strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: extending HJB-based continuous-time RL from single-agent to multi-agent (CT-MARL) settings using PINNs.

The proposed Value Gradient Iteration (VGI) module is a reasonable and interesting mechanism to improve gradient fidelity in PINN-based value learning without requiring ground-truth gradient supervision, addressing a known PINN failure mode (poor gradient backpropagation from sparse boundary conditions).

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple benchmark families (continuous-time MPE, continuous-time multi-agent MuJoCo, and a custom coupled-oscillator environment with analytical LQR ground truth for interpretable validation).
Good set of ablations: VGI on/off, activation function choice, loss-term weighting, and robustness to varying time intervals, which help build a coherent story supporting design choices.

The didactic oscillator experiment with closed-form LQR ground truth is a nice touch, providing interpretable visual/quantitative evidence (Fig. 1, 3, 9) that VGI meaningfully improves value/gradient accuracy over the no-VGI ablation.
Provides theoretical scaffolding (HJB derivation, advantage definition, policy improvement, VGI contraction) which, while not airtight, shows the authors attempted to ground the method formally.
weaknesses: Baselines are weak and outdated for a top-tier venue: DPI and IPI both originate from a single 2021 single-agent paper (Lee & Sutton) and CT-MBRL (ODE) is also a single-agent method; the manuscript does not clearly explain how these were extended/adapted to the CTDE multi-agent setting, raising concerns about baseline implementation fidelity and fairness of comparison.

No comparison against standard, strong discrete-time MARL baselines (e.g., MADDPG, MAPPO, QMIX) across the main benchmark suite; MADDPG only appears in a single robustness plot (Fig. 8), which undercuts the claim that CT-MARL 'consistently outperforms' relevant alternatives.
HJB-PPO [27], a directly relevant PINN+RL baseline discussed extensively in Related Work, is never empirically compared against, despite being closely related prior art.

Some theoretical results are loosely derived: Lemma 3.3's proof assumes an exact greedy policy-improvement argmax at each step, which is inconsistent with the lemma's stated setting of 'one gradient step with sufficiently small step size'; several HJB derivations rely on informal Taylor expansions with approximate equalities rather than rigorous error bounds.

Theorem 3.4's contraction argument is a fairly standard/simple linear-operator contraction result contingent on the time step being sufficiently small; its practical implications for training stability at the actual (non-infinitesimal) step sizes used in experiments are not clearly established.

Novelty relative to prior differential-game value-gradient work (Zhang et al., refs 50 and 51) is incremental; the core idea of tying value learning to gradient learning for PINN-based HJB solving is already established, and VGI's contribution mainly replaces supervised ground-truth gradients with a bootstrapped self-consistent target.

Reliance on learned dynamics and reward models to compute the VGI target introduces compounding approximation errors that are not directly ablated or analyzed (e.g., sensitivity to model quality/error).

No real-world or physically realistic high-dimensional multi-agent task; MuJoCo/MPE variants are synthetic proxies for continuous-time interaction and the significance of results to genuinely high-frequency or irregular real-world control is not demonstrated.
Terminology inconsistency between the paper's framing as a CT-MARL framework and the introduced method name VIP may create confusion; presentation could be tightened.
Limited scope acknowledged by authors (cooperative-only, no competitive or general-sum CT-MARL), which somewhat narrows the practical significance of the contribution for broader MARL research.
